subtopic_detail: choosing between a hydrolysed and an amino acid based formula for an infant with blood streaked stools, eczema and centile loss
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 4 month old girl who was changed from breast to a standard cow's milk based formula at six weeks of age when her mother returned to work.

Since then she has vomited a small amount after most feeds, cries and draws her legs up during and after feeding, and passes six or seven loose stools a day that her mother describes as having streaks of blood in the mucus. The vomits are not forceful and have never been green. She has widespread dry itchy patches on her face and the creases of her elbows and knees that have not improved on twice daily moisturiser and intermittent hydrocortisone. Her weight has fallen from the fiftieth centile at six weeks to the fifteenth centile today. She is afebrile and there have been no sick contacts.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, blood pressure 82/48, respiratory rate 36, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and well perfused, eczema over face and flexures, abdomen soft with no mass, no palpable pylorus, anus normal with no fissure
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and C reactive protein within normal limits, stool culture negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her feeding?

options.text: Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula and review her in two to four weeks
options.rationale: An extensively hydrolysed formula is the first line replacement for non immunoglobulin E mediated cow's milk protein allergy and is tolerated by around nine in ten affected infants, so it is the trial that both treats and confirms the diagnosis. Symptoms of the gastrointestinal type typically settle within two to four weeks, which sets the review interval. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.text: Change to a soy protein based formula and review her again in two to four weeks
options.rationale: Soy formula is not recommended under six months of age, and a substantial minority of infants with the non immunoglobulin E mediated form react to soy protein as well, so the trial frequently fails. It has a limited place in older infants whose families decline a hydrolysate. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.text: Change to an amino acid based formula and review her again in two to four weeks
options.rationale: An amino acid formula is reserved for infants who fail an extensively hydrolysed formula, or who have anaphylaxis, severe enteropathy or faltering growth with hypoalbuminaemia, because it costs several times more and tastes markedly worse. Starting with it skips the step that succeeds in the large majority. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.text: Change to a lactose free formula and review her symptoms in two to four weeks
options.rationale: Removing lactose leaves the cow's milk protein in the feed, and it is the protein that drives the blood streaked stools and the eczema. Primary lactose intolerance is vanishingly rare in infancy and would not cause rectal bleeding or a skin manifestation. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Change to a thickened anti reflux formula and review her again in two to four weeks
options.rationale: Thickening reduces the volume of visible posseting but does nothing for the colitis causing the blood and mucus or for the eczema, and reflux alone does not cause centile loss of this degree. The blood streaked stool is the finding that moves the diagnosis away from uncomplicated reflux. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Cow's milk protein allergy splits into an immunoglobulin E mediated form with rapid onset urticaria, angioedema, vomiting or anaphylaxis, and a non immunoglobulin E mediated form with delayed gastrointestinal and skin manifestations, of which proctocolitis and enteropathy are the commonest patterns in infancy. Skin prick testing and specific immunoglobulin E are useful only for the immediate form and are normal in the delayed form, so the diagnosis rests on an elimination and challenge sequence rather than on a laboratory test. Improvement on elimination must be followed by a planned reintroduction, because a substantial proportion of infants labelled allergic on elimination alone are not, and unnecessary formula restriction is expensive and nutritionally limiting. Where a mother is still breastfeeding, maternal dairy exclusion with calcium and vitamin D supplementation is preferred over stopping breastfeeding. Most children outgrow the non immunoglobulin E mediated form by two to three years of age, so a structured reintroduction plan is part of initial management rather than an afterthought.
key_points: Delayed gastrointestinal and skin symptoms define the non immunoglobulin E mediated form
Specific immunoglobulin E testing is normal in the delayed form and does not exclude it
Extensively hydrolysed formula is first line and works for around ninety per cent
Soy is avoided under six months and cross reacts in a significant minority
Confirm the diagnosis with a planned reintroduction rather than leaving the label unchallenged
explanation.pearls: Blood streaked mucous stools in an otherwise thriving, afebrile infant is the signature of allergic proctocolitis, and it characteristically resolves within two to four weeks of removing the protein, which is much faster than the eczema improves.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: the silent sight threatening complication that must be screened for in a young girl with a persistently swollen knee and a positive antinuclear antibody
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4 year old girl who has limped for four months. Her mother says she is at her worst first thing in the morning and hobbles for about an hour before loosening up, and that she is back to running by the afternoon.

There was no injury. She has had no fevers, no rash, no weight loss and no night pain that wakes her. Her right knee has been visibly swollen throughout and she has begun to keep it slightly bent when standing. She has no eye pain, no redness and no photophobia, and her mother has noticed nothing wrong with her vision. The rheumatology team has confirmed a diagnosis of oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis and is starting an intra articular corticosteroid injection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right knee warm with an effusion and a 10 degree fixed flexion deformity, no other joint involved, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, white eyes with no injection
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5), full blood count within normal limits, antinuclear antibody positive at 1 in 320, rheumatoid factor negative

lead_in: What additional step is most important in her ongoing care?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the right knee to assess for synovial thickening
options.rationale: Imaging can characterise synovitis and is used where the diagnosis is uncertain or a single joint behaves unusually, but the diagnosis is already established and the result would not change treatment. It also requires sedation at this age for no additional benefit. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Aspiration of the knee effusion for cell count, Gram stain and bacterial culture
options.rationale: Aspiration is essential when infection is a possibility, but four months of morning stiffness that eases through the day in an afebrile child with a mildly raised inflammatory marker is not a septic picture. Fluid will be obtained in any case when the joint is injected. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Testing for human leucocyte antigen B27 to define the arthritis subtype further
options.rationale: This marker is associated with enthesitis related arthritis, which typically affects older boys with lower limb enthesitis and sacroiliac involvement and causes an acute painful red eye rather than a silent one. It would not alter the surveillance that this girl's own subtype demands. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association

options.text: Slit lamp examination by an ophthalmologist arranged within the next few weeks
options.rationale: Chronic anterior uveitis in this subtype is asymptomatic with a white eye and normal vision until irreversible damage has occurred, so it is detectable only on slit lamp examination and is screened for regardless of symptoms. Young age at onset, oligoarticular disease and a positive antinuclear antibody together place her in the highest risk group. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association

options.text: Visual acuity assessment at each clinic visit performed by the practice nurse
options.rationale: Acuity remains normal until the uveitis has already produced posterior synechiae, cataract or band keratopathy, so relying on it means detecting the complication only once sight has been lost. The distinction from the correct answer is that only the slit lamp can see the anterior chamber cells that come first. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association

explanation.summary: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is defined as arthritis beginning before the sixteenth birthday and persisting for at least six weeks with no other identified cause, and the oligoarticular subtype involving four or fewer joints is the commonest presentation in Australian children. It characteristically affects young girls, favours the knee, and produces morning stiffness that improves with activity, which is the opposite of the pattern seen in mechanical or malignant bone pain. Chronic anterior uveitis complicates up to a fifth of cases in this subtype and is uniquely dangerous because it is entirely asymptomatic, with a white quiet eye and preserved acuity, until complications develop. Risk is highest in girls, in those under seven at onset, in oligoarticular disease and in those with a positive antinuclear antibody, and these factors determine screening frequency rather than whether to screen at all. Untreated uveitis causes posterior synechiae, cataract, glaucoma, band keratopathy and permanent visual loss, and remains a leading cause of avoidable childhood blindness.
key_points: Morning stiffness easing with activity distinguishes inflammatory from mechanical joint pain
Chronic anterior uveitis in this subtype is asymptomatic with a white eye
Only slit lamp examination detects it early; acuity is normal until damage is done
Positive antinuclear antibody, young onset and oligoarticular disease mark the highest risk group
A red painful photophobic eye instead suggests the enthesitis related subtype
explanation.pearls: Highest risk children, meaning those under seven at onset with a positive antinuclear antibody, need slit lamp screening every three months for the first four years, not annually, and screening continues for years after the arthritis itself has gone quiet.

subtopic_detail: whether a sleep study is required before surgical referral in an otherwise well preschooler with classic obstructive symptoms and large tonsils
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 5 year old boy whose parents are worried about his breathing at night. He has snored every night for two years and they now hear him stop for several seconds and then gasp, several times an hour.

He sleeps with his neck extended and his mouth open, thrashes about, and sweats through his pyjamas. He was dry at night for eight months and has been wetting the bed again for the past four. His kindergarten teacher has raised concerns that he is inattentive and cannot sit still at mat time. His weight and height are both on the fiftieth centile. He has no craniofacial abnormality, no neuromuscular disorder and no chromosomal condition, and his tonsils touch in the midline on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, blood pressure 98/60, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tonsils meeting in the midline, mouth breathing, no adenoid facies, chest clear, heart sounds dual with no murmur, body mass index on the fiftieth centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange overnight oximetry at home and refer only if desaturations are recorded
options.rationale: Oximetry has reasonable specificity but poor sensitivity in children, so a normal study is uninterpretable and cannot be used to withhold referral. Making referral conditional on it means a proportion of genuinely affected children are turned away. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Arrange laboratory polysomnography and refer once the study confirms the diagnosis
options.rationale: A formal sleep study is required where the picture is atypical or where surgery carries higher risk, meaning children under two, obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial anomaly or neuromuscular disease, none of which applies to him. Insisting on it in a straightforward case adds months of waiting for a study that would not change the plan. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Commence an intranasal corticosteroid with montelukast and review in three months
options.rationale: Anti inflammatory treatment has a role in mild disease or in children awaiting surgery, and montelukast carries a recognised risk of neuropsychiatric adverse effects that must be discussed with families. Witnessed apnoea with secondary enuresis is beyond the severity at which a medical trial is appropriate as the sole plan. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory

options.text: Refer to an otolaryngologist for consideration of adenotonsillectomy without delay
options.rationale: In an otherwise healthy child over two with a classic obstructive history and tonsils meeting in the midline, adenotonsillectomy is the first line treatment and the diagnosis can be made clinically, so referral proceeds without a sleep study. Surgery resolves symptoms in the large majority and improves the behavioural and nocturnal enuresis features as well. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Refer to a sleep physician for assessment for nocturnal continuous positive pressure
options.rationale: Positive airway pressure is the treatment for children who have residual disease after surgery or who cannot have surgery, and adherence in preschoolers is difficult. It is not offered before the adenotonsillar tissue that is causing the obstruction has been dealt with. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Obstructive sleep apnoea affects around two to four per cent of children and peaks between two and eight years when adenotonsillar tissue is largest relative to the airway. The nocturnal history is the diagnostic core: habitual snoring every night, witnessed pauses, gasping, restless sleep, sweating, unusual sleeping positions with the neck extended, and secondary nocturnal enuresis after a period of dryness. Daytime consequences in children are more often inattention, hyperactivity and irritability than the frank sleepiness seen in adults, and children are not infrequently assessed for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder before the breathing is considered. Australian practice accepts a clinical diagnosis in the otherwise well child over two with a typical history and large tonsils, reserving polysomnography for the higher risk groups in whom surgical risk and the likelihood of residual disease are greater. Untreated disease causes growth impairment, behavioural and learning difficulty, and in severe cases pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain.
key_points: Habitual snoring with witnessed apnoea and restless sleep is the diagnostic history
Secondary nocturnal enuresis after established dryness is a recognised feature
Children present with inattention and hyperactivity rather than daytime sleepiness
Polysomnography is reserved for under twos, obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial and neuromuscular disease
Adenotonsillectomy is first line in the otherwise healthy child with large tonsils
explanation.pearls: Children under three, and those with severe disease or comorbidity, need overnight postoperative monitoring after adenotonsillectomy because respiratory complications cluster in the first night, so day surgery is not appropriate for that group.

subtopic_detail: separating nutritional from inherited phosphate wasting rickets in a toddler with worsening bow legs using the parathyroid hormone level
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 20 month old boy in Melbourne whose mother is worried that his legs are becoming more bowed rather than less. He began walking at seventeen months and tires quickly.

He was breastfed exclusively until fourteen months and has never received a vitamin supplement. He now eats family foods but refuses dairy. His mother has deeply pigmented skin and wears clothing that covers her arms and legs when outdoors, and he spends most days indoors at home. There is no family history of short stature, bone disease or bowed legs in either parent. On examination his wrists are widened, there are palpable beading swellings along his costochondral junctions, and his forehead is prominent. His length is on the third centile having previously tracked along the twenty fifth.

data_table.Examination: Widened wrists, costochondral beading, frontal bossing, symmetrical genu varum with an intercondylar distance of 7 cm, no limb asymmetry
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.13 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.55), phosphate 0.85 mmol/L (1.20 to 2.20), alkaline phosphatase 1180 U/L (100 to 350), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 16 nmol/L (greater than 50), parathyroid hormone 16.4 pmol/L (1.6 to 6.9), creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for bracing of both legs with review of the angle in six months
options.rationale: The deformity is a consequence of unmineralised growth plate cartilage and it remodels once the metabolic defect is corrected, so bracing treats the visible sign while the bone disease continues. Orthopaedic input is reserved for deformity that persists after biochemical correction. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Commence high dose colecalciferol with adequate dietary or supplemental calcium
options.rationale: A 25 hydroxyvitamin D of 16 nmol/L with secondary elevation of parathyroid hormone, low phosphate and a high alkaline phosphatase is nutritional deficiency, and replacing the vitamin with sufficient calcium substrate heals the growth plate over weeks to months. Calcium must accompany the vitamin because rapid remineralisation otherwise drives the calcium down further. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Commence oral phosphate supplements with calcitriol and monitor renal ultrasound
options.rationale: This is the treatment for inherited phosphate wasting rickets, in which vitamin D and parathyroid hormone are both normal and the phosphate is low in isolation. Here both the profoundly low vitamin D level and the elevated parathyroid hormone point to a nutritional rather than a renal tubular cause. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Commence an oral calcium supplement alone and repeat his biochemistry in three months
options.rationale: Calcium alone does not correct the underlying deficiency of the vitamin needed to absorb it, so the parathyroid drive and the growth plate disease persist. Calcium is a necessary companion to the vitamin rather than a treatment in its own right here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Reassure that this is physiological bowing and arrange review at three years of age
options.rationale: Physiological genu varum is symmetrical, painless, improves after about eighteen months and comes with entirely normal biochemistry and no metaphyseal signs. Widened wrists, costochondral beading, falling length centiles and an alkaline phosphatase of 1180 U/L are incompatible with it. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Nutritional rickets remains present in Australia despite abundant sunlight, concentrated in children with deeply pigmented skin, in those whose mothers were deficient during pregnancy, in prolonged exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation, and in families whose cultural dress or indoor lifestyle limits ultraviolet exposure. Breast milk contains very little vitamin D, so an exclusively breastfed infant depends on maternal stores and on supplementation. The biochemical sequence is a fall in vitamin D leading to reduced calcium absorption, a compensatory rise in parathyroid hormone that defends the calcium at the expense of phosphate wasting, and a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase from the unmineralised growth plate. That pattern of low or low normal calcium with low phosphate and high parathyroid hormone is what separates it from inherited phosphate wasting disease, where parathyroid hormone and vitamin D are normal. Radiographs of the wrist or knee show cupping, fraying and widening of the metaphysis and confirm the diagnosis when it is in doubt.
key_points: Low vitamin D with a raised parathyroid hormone defines the nutritional form
Normal parathyroid hormone with isolated low phosphate suggests inherited phosphate wasting
Alkaline phosphatase is markedly raised and is the most sensitive screening test
Calcium must be given with the vitamin to avoid a fall during remineralisation
Deformity remodels after biochemical healing and rarely needs orthopaedic correction
explanation.pearls: Australian guidance recommends 400 international units of vitamin D daily for infants at risk, including exclusively breastfed babies of mothers who are deficient, and the same at risk groups need maternal supplementation through pregnancy and lactation.

subtopic_detail: persistent delayed sleep onset in an autistic school aged child after a documented adequate trial of behavioural sleep measures
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 8 year old autistic boy whose parents say bedtime has become the hardest part of the day. Lights go out at half past seven and he is still awake at half past nine or later, almost every night.

Over the past three months the family has worked with a psychologist on a written plan: the same routine every night, screens off an hour before bed, a dark and quiet bedroom, no daytime naps, morning outdoor light and a consistent wake time. His parents have kept a diary showing they followed it and that sleep onset latency has not changed. Once asleep he stays asleep and wakes at half past five. He does not snore, has no witnessed pauses in breathing and has no urge to move his legs at night. He takes no regular medication, his ferritin is normal and he has never had a stimulant prescribed.

data_table.Examination: Tonsils small, body mass index on the fiftieth centile, neurological examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 48 micrograms/L (20 to 200), full blood count and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for overnight polysomnography before considering any medication for sleep
options.rationale: A sleep study is indicated when the history suggests sleep disordered breathing or a periodic limb movement disorder, and the absence of snoring, apnoea and leg symptoms with small tonsils and a normal ferritin makes those unlikely. His problem is initiating sleep rather than maintaining it. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Prescribe promethazine at bedtime and review his sleep diary again in four weeks
options.rationale: Sedating antihistamines produce tolerance within weeks, cause daytime drowsiness and can paradoxically agitate children, and they do not act on the circadian mechanism driving delayed sleep onset. They are not recommended for chronic paediatric insomnia. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Reinforce the existing behavioural plan and review his sleep diary in three months
options.rationale: Behavioural measures are the correct first line and must be in place before and alongside any drug, but a documented three month trial with a diary showing adherence and no change has already tested them. Repeating an intervention that has failed costs the family another term of broken evenings. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Trial melatonin given before bedtime while continuing the behavioural measures
options.rationale: Melatonin has the strongest evidence for delayed sleep onset in autistic children who have not responded to an adequate behavioural programme, reducing sleep latency by around half an hour and increasing total sleep time. It is added to the behavioural measures rather than replacing them, because the combination outperforms either alone. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Prescribe clonidine at night and monitor his blood pressure and pulse at review
options.rationale: Clonidine is used for paediatric sleep problems, particularly where there is coexisting attention deficit hyperactivity disorder being treated with a stimulant, but it requires cardiovascular monitoring and causes rebound on abrupt cessation. It sits behind melatonin in the sequence for an otherwise well child. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Sleep problems affect the majority of autistic children and are among the strongest predictors of parental distress and of daytime behavioural difficulty, so they are worth asking about at every review rather than waiting for them to be raised. Delayed sleep onset is the commonest pattern and is thought to reflect a combination of altered melatonin secretion, heightened arousal and sensory sensitivity. Behavioural intervention is the first line at every age and includes a fixed routine, a consistent wake time, removal of evening screens, attention to bedroom sensory features and management of daytime activity. Before attributing insomnia to autism itself, treatable contributors are excluded: obstructive sleep apnoea, iron deficiency driving restless legs, gastro oesophageal reflux, pain, constipation, epilepsy, anxiety and the effect of stimulant medication given too late in the day. Melatonin is the best studied pharmacological option in this group and is continued alongside rather than instead of the behavioural plan, with periodic trials off treatment.
key_points: Behavioural measures come first and continue after any drug is added
Exclude sleep disordered breathing, iron deficiency, reflux, pain and late stimulant dosing
A normal ferritin makes restless legs an unlikely contributor
Melatonin is the best evidenced pharmacological option for delayed sleep onset in autism
Sedating antihistamines produce tolerance and can cause paradoxical agitation
explanation.pearls: Melatonin is most effective when given about thirty to sixty minutes before the intended bedtime rather than at the time the child currently falls asleep, because the aim is to advance the circadian phase rather than simply to sedate.
